edbDesc: The elastic scattering of light or other electromagnetic radiation by particles much smaller than the wavelength of the light.
title: Rayleigh scattering
description: Air molecules scatter blue light far more than red, so the sky looks blue in every direction and the setting sun, whose light has lost its blue on the long way through the air, looks red. John Tyndall saw blue light scattered by fine haze in the 1860s, and Lord Rayleigh worked out in 1871 that the shorter the wavelength, the much stronger the scattering. It sets how clear optical fibres can be and lets lasers measure the air high above.
effect: particles much smaller than the light's wavelength scatter blue light far more than red
usedIn: Rayleigh lidar that measures upper-air temperature
Light-scattering instruments that weigh polymer molecules
Explains the blue sky and red sunsets
strength: Blue light is scattered about five times more than red; in the best glass fibre it still costs half the light every 20 km or so.
pickWhy: Specific named effect with real measuring jobs; not in the deck (Tyndall's deck card is the greenhouse effect).
